subtopic: INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD- PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF RATE STRUCTURE OF RAILWAYS UNDER JURISDICTION OF PARLIAMENT
INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD- PROPOSED INVESTIGATION OF RATE STRUCTURE OF RAILWAYS UNDER JURISDICTION OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Board of
Transport Commissioners for Canada, by order No. 70425 of March 30, 1948, authorized the member railway companies of the Railway Association of Canada to make a general advance in freight rates of 21 per cent with certain exceptions, and on coal and coke a flat increase of 25 cents per ton.
The railway companies were authorized to publish and file tariff schedules, in accordance with the board's findings, on not less than three days' notice.
The board's authorization for increased rates does not include the following:-
1.	Rates on grain and grain products from all points on all lines of railway west of Fort William to Fort William, Port Arthur and Armstrong.
2.	Rates on grain and grain products from all prairie points on all lines of railway to Vancouver, Prince Rupert and other British Columbia coast ports for export.
3.	Rates on grain and grain products for domestic consumption between points in western Canada and rates on feed grain published in C.F.A. tariff C.T.C. 154.
4.	Joint international rates between Canada and the United States of America (except
coal and coke, board order No. 70462) which were increased as a result of decisions of the interstate commerce commission in ex parte 148, 162 and 166.
5.	Rates between United States points on traffic passing through Canada.
6.	Export and import rates to and from Canadian ports, which are at present on a parity with rates to or from United States ports.
7.	Agreed charges.
8.	Demurrage and penalty charges.
9.	Interswitching rates covered by the board's general order No. 252, dated October 26, 1918.
The government has reviewed the petition from the transportation commission of the maritime board of trade, representing inter alia the governments of the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island and representations made on behalf of the governments of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia and other interested persons and organizations, to vary order No. 70425 of the board of transport commissioners by providing that tariff schedules published and filed under the provisions of this order be not effective until at least thirty days from the date thereof.
After careful consideration of these representations, and, without prejudice to any appeal, the government has decided that it should not interfere with the effective date of the board's order.
The government has taken into consideration the fact that no general investigation of freight rates has been made in Canada since that conducted in 1925 by the board of railway commissioners. In the circumstances, the government has decided it would be in the public interest to have the board of transport commissioners make a thorough investigation of the rate structure of railways and railway companies which are under the jurisdiction of parliament, with a view to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rate structure which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities so as to permit the freest possible exchange of commodities between the various provinces and territories of Canada and the extension of Canadian trade, both foreign and domestic, having due regard
Freight Rates

to the needs of agriculture and other basic industries. This investigation will be subject, of course, to the statutory provisions affecting freight rates known as the Maritime Freight Rates Act and the Crowsnest Pass agreement.
I now table orders in council P.C. 1486 and P.C. 1487 of today's date, giving effect to the decisions of the government.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT ORDERS

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs, for the Prime Minister) moved:
That, notwithstanding any other order passed by the house in relation thereto, on and after Wednesday, the 7th of April and every day thereafter until otherwise ordered during the present session, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence over all other business except the introduction of bills, questions by members and notices of motions for the production of papers, and from 8 to 9 p.m. on Fridays, private bills.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT ORDERS
speechtext:
I desire to say a word on this motion of the Prime Minister which has been moved by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It is
Business oj the House

generally understood, and I think generally accepted in all corners of the house, that normally and naturally a certain right of way should be given to the government in connection with urgent business which it desires to bring before parliament. On that point therefore no grave exception will be taken to the general principle. On the other hand, the situation here is quite different, because the government, I submit, should not take the attitude of hogging procedure, if I may use that expression, with respect to the introduction and discussion of legislation at the expense of private members on all sides of the house. There must be some give and take on both sides. I would not want to see the order paper cluttered up with private members' resolutions at various stages of the session at the expense of urgent government legislation which all of us wish to have passed. Surely, however, there is some happy medium which parliament might adopt. I must confess that I cannot see how the government at this stage of the session can possibly ask parliament to pass a resolution in the precise terms of the motion now before us.
There are thirty-five private members' notices of motions on the order paper. Many of these are of very great importance. In addition there are public bills awaiting consideration. I think the government is asking too much of parliament when it seeks to have this resolution carried in a form which private members on all sides of the house find it impossible to accept.
I wish to make it perfectly clear that any move we make with reference to this resolution is not for the purpose of delaying government business, because we are not asking for very much in what we now seek. I hear an interruption. You people over there would have us get nothing, I suppose, but thank goodness there are members here who want us to get a fair deal.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT ORDERS
speechtext: The interruption came from that side.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT ORDERS
speechtext:
I do not care where it came from. You people will have to take the same criticism because I will criticize fairly wherever criticism is called for.
My suggestion on behalf of the official opposition is this. We are prepared to allow the government to pass this resolution if they will reduce the period to two weeks, because it is not fair to ask parliament to give the government carte blanche, a blank cheque for the whole session, thereby denying private members the right to bring forward important matters from time to time.

If this motion is adopted it will be following a precedent which has been adhered to not only during the war but in sessions since the war. It is about time the government realized that they are not the only ones in the House of Commons who have been sent here by the people of the country.
I submit that the suggestion I offer is a fair and a just one, namely that we change the date mentioned in this resolution, April 7, to two weeks thereafter. Then, if government business demands a further extension, we shall be prepared to consider it, though I believe that by the time the two weeks have elapsed, enough of urgent government business ought to have been passed, so we should at least give private members something of a break. They are entitled to it, and I am speaking on their behalf at the moment. I ask the government to accept this proposal.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the criticism made this afternoon by the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon). I am not sure whether his suggestion to the government is of sufficient advantage or offers sufficient latitude to private members. As he pointed out, there are thirty-five private members' resolutions on the order paper, some of them relating to very important topics of great interest to the country at large. I agree with him that while we were willing to forgo many of the rights and privileges of private members during the war, because of the necessities of that period, we do not feel that we should forgo those rights and privileges now that the war is over.
As a matter of fact, all that this resolution proposed by the Prime Minister allots is the hour from 8 to 9 on Friday evenings, and for private bills only. May I point out that private bills are measures that are of interest to private individuals or to private corporations. They are bills which come before this house, moved by private members, asking for special privileges, often for an individual, as in the case of divorce, or for small groups, associations or corporations. On the other hand, there are a number of public bills on the order paper, and they have to do with matters which are of paramount interest to the public of Canada. True, they are sponsored by private members, but when we look at them we realize how important they are. One or two may be rather embarrassing to the government and may not meet with the approval of some members of the house, but whether they are embarrassing or not, whether we agree with them or not, they are of public importance and should be given precedence

Business oj the House
over bills which relate merely to individuals or to private groups of people. I say whether we agree with them or not, and there are at least two of these bills with which I am in disagreement; nevertheless they are of sufficient importance to warrant their being discussed and decided by the house.
Let us look for a moment at these bills. There is an act to amend the criminal code, moved by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmoreney (Mr. LaCroix). There is an act to amend the Dairy Industry Act, which is a measure dealing with the sale of oleomargarine,-

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT ORDERS
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT ORDERS
speechtext: -something which is important to the country. Whether my hon. friend the member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) and I agree with it or not, it should be discussed and decided by the house.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT ORDERS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT ORDERS
speechtext:
That is where it should be decided. Then there is an act to amend the Supreme Court Act, which deals with appeals to the privy council, and an act to amend the Railway Act, which deals with a very large group of pensioners of one of the railways.
These are public bills the subject matters of which are of widespread interest. Why should private bills be given preference over public bills of such importance?
I am going to move in amendment:
That all the words after the words "production of papers," in the sixth line of the motion, be deleted, and the following be substituted therefor:
"and from 8 to 9 p.m. on Tuesdays and Fridays, public and private bills, the former having precedence."
From 8 to 9 p.m. on Tuesdays and Fridays, restoring the two. hours that are given to bills introduced into this house by private members, public bills having a preference over private bills-the opposite of the motion standing in the name of the Prime Minister and now before the house. I believe the house should support such an amendment.
May I say this before I take my seat. We are not asking for the restoration of all private members' days at this stage of the session, but we do think that the minimum we should ask for is what my amendment to the motion now proposes.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT ORDERS
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on this subject, Mr. Speaker, speaking not as a nominal supporter of the government but as a private member and a backbencher.
We have heard from the leader of the government and leaders of the opposition groups. We as backbenchers may be comparatively insignificant and unimportant as individuals when compared with these leaders, but the rights we have as members of parliament are extremely important and significant, and they have never been more so than they are today. Chief amongst those is a fair allocation to private members of the time of parliament as set forth in standing order 15(3), which says that on Monday, Wednesday, and Thursday for the first four weeks of the session the business of private members shall have precedence over government business. That clearly shows that the intent of our constitution is not that this parliament should be the creature of the government, and not that the time of this parliament should be the monopoly of the government.
It is quiet true that in some countries- Russia for example-the government has the monopoly of. government business, with no opposition. On the other extreme, in the United States, the executive branch of the government has no right to initiate legislation. All legislation is sponsored by private members, if they can be so called, members of congress or the senate. Here under the British system I think we have a middle course, very wisely, in that the government, being the responsible authority in the country, has certain rights in parliament. But so has every backbencher, no matter how distant or remote his riding may be. If we are limited to those subjects which the government cares to bring forward, then we are in this position: we can only support or oppose. Anything which the government does not want to bring before parliament, anything which it ignores, overlooks, or thinks to be unimportant, no matter what our constituents may think, we of course cadnot discuss.
In wartime we gladly gave up certain rights we had as private members, but once the war was over we expected that they would be restored. I looked over the orders of the day for the third session after the last war, in 1921; it is three years now since the end of the second world war. In 1921 the speech from the throne was given the usual precedence over all other business and the debate ended on March 3. March 4 was private members' day. At 3.15 on March 4, without any question or hesitation, a private member from Edmonton started to discuss his resolution. That is the way things went during that session. I looked up the record after the second world war, and found it most interesting. In 1946 the
Business of the House

session began on March 15. On April 3, less than three weeks after the beginning of the session, we were embarked on private members' day, with resolutions and bills. There were five bills and six resolutions debated that session. Three of them came to a vote. In 1947 the session began on January 31. Thi3 time it was not until April 4, two months later, that private members had an opportunity to discuss public bills and resolutions. At that time seven bills and six resolutions were debated. Three were voted upon.
Now in 1948, when we are three years away from the war, after four months of sitting, a motion is proposed the effect of which is to cut off completely any hope of private members' bills cr resolutions coming up for debate.
The government offers the argument-the Prime Minister offered it to me two years ago when I objected to being cut off when the resolution was reached at that time-that ample opportunity is afforded to private members to discuss whatever they wish on the speech from the throne, on the budget or on going into supply. Those opportunities are there, it is true. But what happens in those debates is that every member speaks on a different subject. We are like an army riding off in all directions. Our efforts are dissipated and the government carries on with its own program. If we had our private members' days on which to debate specific problems, then the attention of all members would be fixed on those problems, and bills and resolutions introduced by private members are voted upon. Then the government and the people of the country would know what parliament's feeling is on these matters.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has mentioned the fact that these public bills-and naturally I am greatly interested in one of them, the oleomargarine bill- are not unimportant or trivial. Certainly the first bill, with regard to the outlawing of the communist party, is a subject of great concern across this country. It is quite true that we had a debate on it in parliament lasting one day and leading nowhere. In this country there are a great many people who think that the communist party should be outlawed. There are also a great many people who are not communists but who believe it should not be outlawed. All these people are looking to this parliament for specific direction on that matter-a direction which cannot be avoided by having a three-hour afternoon's blowoff on the subject of communism.
The next thing under public bills and orders is the bill in respect to oleomargarine. The members from Montreal and Quebec tell me

that their mail today consists mostly of letters from people in the lower income groups, protesting first of all against the high price of butter, and secondly-

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT ORDERS
speechtext: If this house adopts this motion, then any question of the supremacy of parliament can be forgotten for the present session. We passed a motion similar to this last December, under which parliament abdicated all its rights, functions and privileges to the executive, who have been ruling the country over the head of parliament since the day this house met in December. As I have said on other occasions, the freedom and liberty of the subject have been surrendered to outside boards and controls so that people are being fined and imprisoned against all the laws which should apply in this country.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT ORDERS
speechtext: Order. I would ask hon. members to be silent, because it is very difficult to hear the hon. gentleman who has the floor. A great deal has been said about the privileges of backbenchers, but I believe freedom of speech should apply to the occupants of the front benches as well.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT ORDERS
speechtext:
As I have said previously, Mr. Speaker, in difficult days such as these I do not object to giving the government of the day reasonable powers, but the private members of parliament are forgotten entirely. We are the forgotten link in parliamentary government in this country, and this applies to those on the government benches as well as those in all other parties in this house. When the private member ceases to function, all
parliamentary government is at an end. What are we doing here? We are surrendering the control of expenditures to these outside bodies. I had a word to say about this when a previous motion was discussed, and I should like to quote two brief sentences from my remarks on another occasion:
All kinds of bodies, over the head of parliament, are spending money like water. Every principle for which the British nation struggled in the old land since the seventeenth century has been surrendered to the political caucuses. Parliament itself, which came into being to ensure that taxes shall be voted only by those who have to pay them, has become the institution through which those who do not pay them impose them on others.
And there is another sentence:
. . . powers of legislation older even than the right of taxpayers to determine the national expenditure have been surrendered, and if we are to continue this sort of thing the power of parliament will be gone for ever.

Quite right, Mr. Speaker; I am directing my remarks to the motion and the amendment.. I say we might as well all go home. It is no wonder the people back home in our constituencies are asking what the members of parliament are doing. They want to know what we are doing in connection with margarine and many other matters that have been mentioned here today, but the answer is nothing at all. It is said we are to have a debate on foreign affairs, but I doubt if we will ever get to it; by that time the empire may be gone.
In conclusion I say these matters of controllers and executive rule affect every man, woman and child in the country, and we have surrendered all these powers to the executive. They are irresponsible. They are irremovable, under no control and subject to no appeal. They are above the law, the courts and the House of Commons. If we are not to have our rights and privileges we might as well turn the key in the door of parliament and go home.

I repeat, as an independent member of this house- infinitely more independent than any member of any of these parties sitting around me, who rally around their whips-I want to add my protest to the form of this resolution. The government must admit that hon. members on all sides have been quite prepared to co-operate in expediting the business of the house, but I think this resolution, which asks us to give up the rights of private members with no guarantee as to the length of time that will be required, is a little unfair. I believe the government should give further consideration to the matter and see if there is not some way in which a limit can be placed on the time during which they may have the power for which they are asking; perhaps it could be for one month.
Personally I should be very glad to grant such power. As has been stated, we have two bills on the order paper which to my mind are extremely important, not only to those of us in the house but to the people of Canada generally. I refer to the bill which would amend the Dairy Industry Act, and the bill sponsored by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency in regard to illegal organizations. I would not like to have members of the press gallery say in the newspapers that the members of this house were afraid to face these two important issues. I would like the privilege of recording my opinions on these matters, and I am sure many other hon. members feel the same way. I would be grateful therefore if the government would let this motion stand and reconsider the matter with a view to seeing whether it cannot be made more acceptable to the backbenchers-which the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) claims he is not-and the ordinary members of the house.

speechtext: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved the third reading of Bill No. 7, respecting emergency payments to assist in meeting increased cost of production of gold.

subtopic: EMERGENCY PAYMENTS TO ASSIST IN MEETING INCREASED COST OP PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Before this bill receives third reading I wish to say a few words. The bill is entitled, "An act respecting emergency payments to assist in meeting increased cost of production of gold." It is based on a policy which I have advocated for every province of Canada. A policy of bonuses, subventions and subsidies would solve all the economic problems of this country and of every province. It would also solve our economic and fiscal problems and the internal problems of this country, and is based on protection. I advocated this policy when I first entered the house. I advocated a policy of farm assistance and assistance for the development of a national fuel supply from the mari-times, and many other economic aids. I advocated a policy of similar grants, bonuses, subventions and subsidies to food products in this
country. I am sorry that in connection with this gold industry this action was not taken years ago in new Ontario.
I remember when the high production costs of power and many other things in an economic way were preventing the development of this particular industry in northern Ontario. At that time Sir Adam Beck brought forward the policy of municipal ownership of electrical power, and we tried to get it for new Ontario. At that time also the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway was being built, and sections had been built into the gold and silver camps. At that time that railway should have been electrified. If that had been done the mines would have had cheaper production costs and cheap light and power. The cost of light and power was one of the main causes of the high production costs there in this particular industry. At one time in the gold mining and other districts the cost of direct current was up to $60 a horsepower at Cochrane. That was under private ownership. If the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, the government-owned transportation system in new Ontario, had been electrified, that country would have had cheaper production costs by one-half and cheap light and power. They would have got it for $9 or S10 a horsepower as against $60. If that had been done the production of gold today would be five times as high as it has been in the past and the production of silver would be about three times as high.
I can only say that the government is adopting the proper policy in giving emergency relief to this particular industry. I hope that the same principle will be carried out in base metal production and in some food products such as milk and other things. If we carried out this system of bonuses, subventions and subsidies for emergency in such days as these it would solve all the economic problems of Canada from coast to coast, in every province, by protection, particularly if it were properly applied.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on third reading of this bill, but in reading over the speech made yesterday by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) I thought that, as one who has been closely associated with the industry for some twenty odd years, I should put on the record a refutation of some of the things which the hon. member said which were not quite fair to labour and management in that industry.
The first point the hon. member made was that there was difficulty at the present time

in getting union agreements in the mining districts. The hon. member said at page 2678 of Hansard'.
The reason I would like that assurance is that the miners' union in the gold industry has been endeavouring unsuccessfully for nearly two years to get a trade union agreement with the operators.
As is generally known, the trouble in the mining districts between management and the labour unions at the present time is that communist organizers came into the camps from the United States and it has been very difficult for the management to come to any agreement with the unions. I can assure the hon. member for Cape Breton South that, once these difficulties are ironed out, the mines will be very glad to make an agreement with their employees.
Then the hon. member said:
I do not suppose in the whole of Canada there is a section of any industry where the hazards are greater than in the gold and nickel mines in northern Ontario.
It has been said by Mr. Longmore, the general manager of the Hollinger mine, and one of the greatest employers of labour in the mining industry, that in the past few years more accidents to miners have happened going to and coming from work than have occurred underground. Outside of the very few spectacular accidents, gold mining is, I think, a pretty safe industry, the management having a fetish for the safety and welfare of their men.
The next point the hon. member dealt with was silicosis. I do not think that in any other place in the world one will find more attention paid to silicosis and greater efforts made to overcome that hazard of mining than in the gold mining industry of Canada. Everybody who knows anything about the industry in Ontario knows that twenty-five cents per man shift is deducted and a special fund has been created by the compensation board to take care of any cases of silicosis. I have yet to learn of any one case brought before the board that was not considered on its merits and the man or men given reasonable treatment.
Then the hon. member made this statement:
If the minister had written into this particular subsidy-it should not be a one-way street; it should rvork both ways-protection for the miners who dig the gold, take the risks and sacrifice their health, it -would partly meet our demands. If the minister had recommended that at least a portion of this subsidy should be used for the purpose of setting up adequate machinery for the diagnosis of silicosis, it would meet with our approval.

I have indicated what the industry has done with regard to silicosis. I am sure that there is no other place in the world where men are better looked after.
Then the hon. member for Cape Breton South said:
There is no such thing as underground exploration.
One has only to go to a gold mine to know that veins have a habit of disappearing, and that a great deal of underground exploration has to be done, which is very costly, before the veins are located again. One of the big items in the cost of the gold mine is diamond drilling underground to find the veins which possibly have been lost. The point that I should like to make the most of is found on page 2679 of Hansard. I quote what the hon. member said, as reported at page 2679:

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret I have to do
what I intend to do this afternoon. I had no intention of doing it when I came to the house, but, in view of the statement made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) this afternoon, I wish to say something about his announcement. I feel that in endeavouring to place the review of the freight rates and their equalization before the board of transport commissioners again he is simply shelving the question for a couple of years, during which time the people of Canada will have exceedingly high rates inflicted upon them, and that this house should not tolerate the delay.
This matter, as has been pointed out by various hon. members on all sides of the house, including the government side, is one which is squarely on the doorstep of the government itself. I believe that, in view of the serious effects to our economy, this house should have an opportunity of expressing an opinion about what the government proposes to do and, indeed, about what the government has failed to do. I propose to give the house that opportunity, for I am going to move an amendment to the motion to go into supply. My amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is:
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following be substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that the failure of the government to defer the imposition of the increases in freight rates recently authorized by the board of transport commissioners is inimical to the best interests of the people of Canada; further this house is of the opinion that the government should reconsider this matter and take action to prevent the proposed increases from coming into effect at this time."
The reference again to the board of transport commissioners will be a reference on the basis of certain economic considerations; for that, I take it, is what the equalization of freight rates really involves. The speech which I made on Monday afternoon did not deal with economic considerations. It dealt primarily with political considerations; that is to say, on the effects which the board order would have on various areas of Canada in relation to other areas within our country. I said it was a threat to the continuance of good relationships between the various regions of Canada. I said
Freight Rates

it might undermine the very basis of confederation upon which this country was founded. I said it would cause discontent because it would impose upon groups of people who live in the more remote areas a charge which was unfair when that imposition was considered in relation to its effect on people who live in other areas in Canada. I said the judgment of the board of transport commissioners on the basis of cold railroad economics was unjust, unfair, and prejudicial to people who live, as I put it, in the maritimes, in British Columbia and in the prairie provinces.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) has already, I believe, received protests from seven premiers of seven provinces of Canada asking that the new rates be not permitted to go into effect until seven of the nine federated provinces of Canada shall have had an opportunity of placing their representations before the authority which has the right and the obligation to make the final decision in this matter-the federal cabinet of this country.
I say, Mr. Speaker, this house should have the opportunity of expressing itself on this issue. While I regret very much having to delay our going into supply to provide an opportunity which we all want to discuss external affairs on Monday next, this issue is of such importance to the whole of Canada that I believe it should be discussed and decided by the house. I believe in responsible government. I believe that the government of this country should be responsible to this house, just as in turn we are responsible to the people of Canada.
I realize that the amendment which I have moved to the motion to go into supply and which I believe to be entirely in order may mean a vote of want of confidence in the government because of the action it has taken today. I realize what may flow from that vote if the government is defeated, but I want to say to the government that if those consequences should flow this question is of such vital importance to the people of Canada that it should be decided by the people of Canada if necessary.
In moving the amendment, I make it abundantly clear that I believe that this house must [DOT]accept the responsibility of saying to the government: These rates, unjust, unfair and discriminatory, prejudicial to various parts of Canada, should not go into effect at this time. The government in bringing down the order in council this afternoon, merely to refer again to the same tribunal the question of the equalization of rates, is simply dodging an issue which it must face squarely.

I do not propose to enter into a long debate. I made the case I intended to make on Monday afternoon. But this is a grievance which the people of Canada have, and it is a grievance which should not only be aired but placed squarely before the government so that there can be no dodging of the issue. I have moved the amendment, Mr. Speaker, because I want parliament to decide this issue now.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has done a public service to the people of Canada in raising this question at this time, and I wish to associate myself with what he has said. I would draw the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and all the members of the cabinet to the very serious situation which they have allowed to develop during the last few days. I desire to be very moderate in the language I use on this occasion, but it is a very serious occasion. I believe one would be justified in saying that the government has been guilty of the complete abnegation of democracy in this dominion during the last few days. The dominion government represents the provinces of the Dominion of Canada. The government originally in Ottawa was set in Ottawa by the provinces of Canada to act as an agent for them. Seven of the nine provinces of Canada have on several occasions expressed the strongest disapproval of increasing freight rates in the Dominion of Canada at the present time, and since the judgment of the board was announced increasing freight rates by 21 per cent, I understand that every one of those seven provinces has expressed its disapproval once more. The government in its announcement today has chosen to ride roughshod over the expressed opinion of seven of the sovereign provinces of the Dominion of Canada. That is no small matter, and it will lead to plenty of trouble. The government has apparently developed the idea that it can kick the people of Canada around whichever way it chooses. We have seen that attitude in existence on several occasions in the last few years. The people of Canada are becoming tired of being kicked around. The government seems to have the idea that there is no recourse, that a people like the people of the maritimes and the people of the west simply must take whatever the dominion government chooses to give them and like it. There are means to which these people can have recourse. I should like to warn the members of the government not to drive these people too far. If we once become convinced in the western provinces that it is impossible to live with Ontario and Quebec we shall find some means of doing another thing.

Freight Rates
The people of this dominion must bear in mind that western Canadians are Canadians and are entitled to equal treatment. They do not consist of slaves or menials or peasants; they consist of free men, descendants of free men with free traditions, and if they cannot accomplish the desires of their hearts in the way of fair government by sending representatives to Ottawa, Mr. Speaker, they will be tempted to send representatives somewhere else. That is just how serious it is. And if the members of the cabinet have not had that impressed on them I urge them to take my words seriously because I mean every syllable of what I am saying. Men in my constituency, in my province and in several others are talking in just such terms as that.
Not only has the government disregarded the expressed will of seven sovereign provinces in this dominion, but it has completely disregarded the pleas and requests of organizations of producers from coast to coast in this nation. Farmers' organizations and organizations of producers of every kind have sent in requests. Why, one would think these people were babes whispering in a windstorm for all the attention the dominion government gives to what they say.
May I say one more striking thing? I will wager, Mr. Speaker, that if hon. members were freed from party consideration seventy-five per cent of them would vote against the freight rate increase. I will go farther than that; I will wager that sixty per cent of the present Liberal members of this house, if they were freed from party affiliations, would vote solidly against this increase. Therefore what is the government doing when it is disregarding the will of the members of this house? 'If it is not abrogating democracy, I do not know where one would go to find it. Is there any way in the world in which the will of the Dominion of Canada can be made to reach into the minds of the men who occupy the treasury benches today?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just bought two pairs of new glasses: I think I had better give you one pair of them. I am here, really I am, and I want to join in this debate for a number of reasons. My first reason is to try to review the actual situation that we are up against and perhaps take away some of the emotionalism which has characterized the debate up to the present time. I may say that I regret the statements made by my old and honourable friend, the member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), when he was talking about secession, because, although he did not use that word, that is exactly what he was talking about. That will not help the situation at the present time.
I wish to say something about railway rates, and may I first repeat what I said in this House of Commons the first year I was here? On many occasions I have acted for the railways professionally. Therefore I wish the house, in judging anything I may say, to take that fact into consideration. It may be said that I have some self-interest. At any rate, I wish to make it plain that I have had that connection. Perhaps I should add that I acted for the western coal people and the Alberta government in a rate-finding matter where I was opposed by both railways, so that I have had a bit of experience on both sides.
What is the history of rate-making in this dominion? We built these railways, and at

that time the railways charged exactly what they pleased for the freight services which they were rendering. From that time on, everything has been based upon the revenues derived from freight, while very little regard has been had to passenger service, including the hotels, which for a long time were regarded from the point of view of rate-making purposes largely as an advertising lead for the freight carrying business of the roads.
Then we built other railways and competition then limited the rates. And in every case where there was a dual service to any point it reduced those rates. But while that was done, no reductions were ever made in carrying freight to points where there was no competitive rail.
The next event of major importance was the opening of the Panama canal, which introduced into this subject the first major difference, and that was that rates were altered in order to meet water competition from eastern Canada through the canal and around to Vancouver. That was the second major event which took place.
The third thing that happened was the building of good roads in eastern Canada- I mean the middle east here-and then we had truck competition, which directly affected freight rates to points where this competition could operate by way of roads.
I mention these things for this reason, that when we start dealing with railway rates it is necessary to find out exactly what the present crazy-quilt structure is in connection with our present rates. I am not using that word in any derogatory or contemptuous way, because it is admitted by everybody that it is a crazy-quilt structure. In other words, there is no railway in the dominion today that can tell you how much it costs to haul a ton of goods from here to there. They cannot do so because the structure has not been built in that way.
On one occasion before the railway board, when Mr. Justice Fullerton was the chairman, we spent some time in endeavouring to find out what it. cost to haul a ton of coal from Drumheller or Edmonton or Lethbridge to North Bay and to Toronto. In order to get someone who knew how that might be done, they imported a man who was known as a railway cost accountant. At that time there were only five on the continent and they were all employed by the interstate commerce commission. It was there they received their training because the interstate commerce commission had to a very large extent gone into a new system of trying to find out what costs were and then adding something for the operation. That must have been a dozen years ago

Freight Rates
that I am speaking of, and to my knowledge nothing has ever been done to further studies which I consider necessary along lines of that description.
We now come to the present time. We find that the board of transport commissioners have sat, and to me it is a matter of great regret that they either did not deal with or were not permitted to deal with the question of equalization. I think anyone who wants to be fair will admit that, having regard to present conditions, the railways need more money to operate. Anyone who has not had his charges raised in ten years, granted that there was some reason in them at that time, must have, it seems obvious to me, more financial return to permit operations to be carried on.
I need only point to the Canadian National deficit. I do not know whether it was announced in the house, but I saw it in the newspapers within the last month or so. It is a very high figure-

I have no intention of discussing that further, but we come to this position, and I have been a believer in this for a long time. Granted that they need this money, they do not need to get it all in one place, namely in the maritime provinces and western Canada.
What is the situation with respect to freight? I admit that this will be a puzzler to the board or to the government or to anyone else. While we have had an over-all increase of 21 per cent, I know perfectly well that in this part of Canada, where there is real truck competition, they will never get it. If they do, they will lose their business to the trucks. That is a simple economic statement which is absolutely true. I do not, of course, mean all the business. Some things do not lend themselves to movement by trucks. But trucks are growing. The other day I was on the road and I saw them carrying five or six motorcars each. At one time these cars were all carried by the railways in western Canada. I do not know whether it is true of the maritimes, but they are still carried out there by rail.
What does that mean? Let us assume that this over-all 21 per cent is the proper figure and that that is what is required to put these people on a healthy operating basis. It means that that sum which is necessary, or whatever portion of that sum may be raised, owing to real practical conditions, the practical problems of competition in transportation, will be paid by western Canada and by the maritime provinces.
I submit this therefore. I had no idea that this motion was to be moved or that there would be a debate, but I am firmly convinced that what we need is a complete overhauling of the structure, a complete change in the basis upon which it was built, which, of course, involves equalization between western and eastern rates.
I am not one of those who think, in fact I do not believe that anybody does think, the provinces of Ontario and Quebec are deliberately trying to bleed us. I do not think they are deliberately doing anything of the kind, but at the present moment that thought is entering into this situation. I have been down east a number of times and have been told by the people of Ontario that Ontario is the old milch cow and that we are still feeding on this milch cow. I have not heard that so much lately and I am glad I have not. I can refute it at any time. It is no problem at all.
I well remember working in a law office as a student in the years 1907, 1908 and 1909. I was a final year student. I was paid the magnificent or munificent sum of $25 a month, which is not quite as much as is received by the miners about whom the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) is so greatly worried. All I did then was to make out mortgages on land, 90 per cent of them on farm land. I never drew a mortgage in the hundreds and hundreds which I wrote-we could not typewrite them under the law, in those days; they had to be written by hand, those private portions-nor did I see one at less than eight per cent; and I drew many at nine per cent. Then we had tough times in western Canada. We had foreclosures and all that sort of thing.
In eastern Canada the comparable interest rate for the kind of loan I am speaking of was five per cent and not above six per cent. In other words, there was at least a two per cent or three per cent differential. The answer that was given was a sound one. It was that this is new country, the risk is greater; therefore the principle of the larger return applies on account of that risk. What happened? The west paid its interest for a long time and paid it at eight per cent and at nine per cent. Then we had drought and trouble, and we did not get our crops; so we had foreclosures and so on. Then we were told about the tremendous losses made by the eastern loan companies because they had been foolish enough to lend their money in western Canada. Mr. Speaker, they never lost a cent in the aggregate. If, when going into a risky venture they would

make the ordinary business move that a cobbler become a shoemaker would make, they would set up a reserve. If there were more risks, he would set up his reserve. And if that reserve, on the differential in the interest rate, had been set up as it should have been, instead of being put into large buildings and investments of one kind or another, the people who lent money in western Canada on real estate would not have been out one five-cent piece. So we are not so hard on the old milch cow as some people in this eastern part of the country seem to think.

We took a tub of ice cream as a sample. I went to the freight people of the railroad and found out the difference. I am not going to give the figures from memory, but the difference was considerable; in fact I think the one rate was almost double for the same haul. I asked why this should be; and to prove that I have not been talking nonsense about how the rate structure is made, they told me it was because of the truck competition between Edmonton and Drumheller.
It does seem to me that in this country we should not have a rate structure built on such shifting sands, such changeable conditions as I have outlined. Now the government of Alberta is building that road, and of course the freight and package rates will drop right down, so that eventually I am quite sure we shall have a position similar to what we would have if we were shipping to Drumheller, let us say.
What is the answer to this whole problem? I repeat that I do not think we can expect the railways to carry on when for the last ten years they have had no increase in their rates.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Not since 1920.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
Then it is much longer than I said. I do not think in this House of Commons we are the kind of people who would say they just must do this. Wages and all other costs are rising. I do not want to speak of wages only, though I did notice that if he was correctly reported in the newspapers Mr. Mosher said the increase was not enough because the men are at present seeking an increase, and I know a board has been sitting in Montreal dealing with that very matter. Mr. Mosher said the increase was not sufficient to give the men the additional wages to which they thought they were entitled. We cannot just brush off these things. I can see that the minister has a tough problem, and I do not know how he is going to deal with it. I am afraid I have not been a great deal of help, though I have tried to discuss the matter fairly and without pointing at or naming anyone else. But I do say there is not much use in monkeying with the rates, allowing or refusing increases, without at the same time ironing out the inequalities which exist. Someone may say, what about the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, which took no part before this board in those proceedings which were a boon to
my profession; if I had not been in the House of Commons I might have been in them myself? As I say, however, that is a situation which really needs to be remedied.
But supposing we refuse this application today. What will it mean? We are going to pay the Canadian National deficit anyway. We are paying $23,000,000 for this year, one of the biggest years they have ever known. If they do not get more revenue from the people with whom they deal and for whom they transport goods we shall have to pay the difference from the taxes of the people of Canada. It is just as plain as that; there can be no doubt whatever about it.
Then what should we do? I agree with much that has already been said, particularly the remarks of the hon. member for Lethbridge. I do not consider it fair to the people, nor do I consider it fair to the board of transport commissioners themselves, that they should be asked to accept the directive which has been issued. I know some of those men; in fact the chairman is a distant relative by marriage. I know that a person sitting in a judicial position, who appreciates the responsibilities that position carries, does not want to be placed in a position where he might be even suspected of reviewing something he has already done. That just does not belong in the administration of justice, or the administration of law if some people like that word better.
In my opinion our great and main problem is equalization, though I find it very difficult to see that we in the west will be helped substantially when you get to the end of that road, when I know, or at least I think I know, that if the railway companies meet truck competition here in the east they will have to do so at a lower rate than whatever horizontal advance may be permitted in the general rates. As I have said, I appreciate that it is a difficult problem-, but I am going to go farther and say I think it is a responsibility the government must assume. More -than that, it is a responsibility this House of Commons must -assume. While some of us come from one part of the country and others come from another, I think this house can shake off sectionalism in a matter of this kind. Surely we do not want to buy votes in the places where we live because we are helping people purely in- a financial way, while on -the other hand we realize that some increase may be necessary. This may mean the profit making, if you like, and the better operation of our railways; and heaven knows they are far enough behind now. For example, in passenger service they do not even compare with the trains across the line.: - But
Freight Rates

surely we can say we believe this is right. Did it ever occur to anyone in this house to think what would happen to the economy of this country if both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National went broke? Let us not blind ourselves to the real situation.
As I said, equalization is the main problem. I know we in the west and you in the mari-times are carrying too much of the load now; and I know if we do not have equalization, when this is over we shall be carrying not only more of the load but a greater percentage of the load1, which is utterly unfair. I am not going to secede with my good friend the hon. member for Lethbridge; but, though I hate superlatives, I say I think the equalization of freight rates is one of the most urgent matters to be undertaken in this country. If they are equal, who can complain? If they are discriminatory, as they are now, they sow disunity; and as the hon. member for Lethbridge said, disunity is growing in the part of the country from1 which we come.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Question.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
Don't get in too great a rush. I agree wholeheartedly with what has been said by my colleague the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith); and in his summation of the situation I think he has left no doubt in the minds of hon. members of this house as to where our party stands with respect to the question of freight rates. Let me reiterate what I said the other day, that the responsibility for the elimination of discrimination in freight rates rests with the government, or with this house if you like that better; after all, the government is pretty well the house, and we must accept that fact. Here we have a board set up to hear a certain case. It is in the position of a judge, a tribunal to hear arguments for and against a certain matter. Let me repeat what I said the other day, that the best accountants and the best legal minds in the various provinces were chosen to place this question before that tribunal. They did so. As a result of what they brought forth, the board made a decision.
Members in the house from various sections of the country, east and west, have seen fit to take Ontario and Quebec to task because those provinces were not represented at the hearings. I would say that if those governments had had anything at stake in the hearings they would have been represented.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Would the hon. member-

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
Let me say to the hon. member from Nova Scotia that the people there felt they had something at stake, with the result that they were represented. Ontario and Quebec, on the other hand, were not. But the fact of their attitude and the further fact that they were not represented do not mean that the people of Ontario and Quebec are less union-minded than the people in other provinces. We are just as much interested in this national union as any people could be.
I look back over the years and I can remember various situations which developed where help was needed either in the east or in the west. Never once in the years I have sat in the House of Commons have I heard a member from Ontario or Quebec deny to the other provinces of Canada anything we thought was in the best interests^ of the country. Never have I heard a member from Ontario or Quebec in the days of depression say we should not have done this or have done that for the wheat farmers in the drought areas of western Canada.
I have found that in the House of Commons members have been willing to bury their differences, so far as geographical position was concerned; I have found they have been only to O' willing to do anything which would unite more solidly than ever the various provinces. So I say, when hon. members criticize the two central provinces they are doing something to create national disunity rather than to build unity in Canada.
Let us deal with the problem in a big and broad way, considering what is best and in the interests of the country. Again I say: Certainly there are discriminatory rates. I have no hesitation in saying I do not think a man who lives in Lethbridge, Regina or Edmonton should have to pay $200 or $250 more for a Chevrolet than I pay for one in Ontario.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: That is the way to talk.

maintopic: FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
I have no hesitation in saying that perhaps the burden is not proportionately distributed across the country. But that was not the question placed before the board of transport commissioners. The question they had to decide was: Do the railways need more money in order to carry on? Their judgment was that those railways needed 21 per cent more.
The question of discrimination is one of government policy. The other day the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) said the board was a creature of parliament. It is a creature of the government which appointed it-the

Freight Rates
present government. It is not a creature of parliament at all. I say it is the creature of the majority of members in parliament, the majority which constitutes the government of the day. If the government is not prepared to bring in legislation such as would eliminate this discrimination in freight rates, then surely we cannot blame the board of transport commissioners or the provinces of Ontario or Quebec. We must place the blame where it belongs, and that is on the government. They are the ones who should amend the Railway Act, so that this discrimination will be ended, so that a proper share of the burden of freight rates will be distributed across the whole country, and so that the per capita responsibility in respect of freight rates will be better equalized.
When I read the amendment offered by the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell) I agree with my colleague the hon. member for Calgary West when he says that we cannot say to the board, after those months and months of careful consideration, and after all the money and time that have been spent in placing the facts before it, "You must reconsider your decision. The government is now going to take the power to say that the decision shall not come into force." Surely we would look ridiculous if we were to do anything like that, particularly when, as the minister has said, the board is the creature of parliament or, as I say, of the government.
But the government has every right to say, "We will reconsider the Railway Act; we will reconsider the question of the equalization of freight rates, and their equal distribution across the country." If the government does that I think we shall have brought to an end this unfortunate situation in which we find men from the maritimes and the west attacking the two central provinces, and leaving the impression across the country that the two central provinces are milking the rest of the country in the matter of freight rates.
This question is not the responsibility of the central provinces at all. They do not make the rates, nor do they appoint the board of transport commissioners. It just happens that Ontario and Quebec are situated as they are, and that the question of freight rates is one entirely within federal jurisdiction and one over which the provinces have no control.
On motion of Mr. Homuth the debate was adjourned.

What is the business for tomorrow?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Tomorrow we shall take up second reading of Bill No. 195 concerning the investigation, conciliation and settlement of industrial disputes. Following that, we shall take second reading of Bill No. 196, to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act; then the resolution standing in the name of the Secretary of State for the introduction of a bill to amend the elections act. Following that, we shall' consider the resolution standing in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, having for its purpose the introduction of a bill to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act, and the order in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce for the second reading of Bill No. 138, to amend the Export and Import Permits Act.

When will this debate be resumed?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: We shall now have to consider what would be the convenient time to resume this debate. Of course the debate on external affairs cannot go on until this debate has been disposed of.
I understand that, and I regret it.
